name: Calvin Coolidge
summary: Coolidge was a Republican small-government conservative who favored low taxes, balanced budgets, a protective tariff, restricted immigration and light business regulation. He defended constitutional limits, representative government and obedience to law, supported women's suffrage and federal action against lynching, and kept the US out of the League of Nations while backing the World Court and the Kellogg-Briand pact.

abolish-hereditary-privilege.rationale: Stated that no one is born into a superior station and there is to be no ruling class.

abolish-income-tax.rationale: He championed and signed the Revenue Acts of 1924 and 1926, which lowered rates while keeping the income tax as a source of federal revenue.

abolish-wage-labour.rationale: He signed the Railway Labor Act, establishing procedures under which railroads and their employees could bargain over rates of pay.

all-land-state-owned.rationale: In discussing wartime housing he endorsed Massachusetts’s program to help citizens acquire real estate and said temporary public possession should leave ownership with private owners.

arbitrator-settles-disputes.rationale: His administration hosted the inter-American arbitration conference and signed its treaty requiring arbitration of eligible international legal disputes that diplomacy could not settle.

arms-reduction.rationale: Backed the Washington naval limitation treaty and wanted further agreements to reduce the waste of armament competition, while insisting on adequate defense.

avoid-deficit-stimulus.rationale: His administration maintained budget surpluses and used them to reduce federal debt while cutting taxes.

ban-cartels.rationale: In his Massachusetts addresses he defended antitrust law and the state’s authority to disperse unlawful combinations of capital.

capitalism-progressive.rationale: Credited industry and enterprise with creating national wealth, attracting immigration and driving progress, and defended the profit system.

central-planning.rationale: Warned that paternalism and bureaucratic supervision of every activity kill initiative; rejected socialism and public ownership.

civilizing-tutelage.rationale: Said the country extended its domain over distant islands and accepted an obligation to bestow justice and liberty on less favored peoples.

class-collaboration.rationale: Said industry cannot flourish if labor languishes and that employer and workman must each contribute; warned strikes embitter and divide the nation into warring classes.

collective-bargaining.rationale: He signed the Railway Labor Act, which protected railroad workers’ organization and established collective bargaining procedures for rates of pay and working conditions.

consent-of-governed.rationale: Called it final that governments derive their just powers from the consent of the governed.

constitutional-jury-trial.rationale: In The Destiny of America he praised the protection afforded by requiring an impartial jury’s verdict before the federal government could convict someone of a crime.

correct-racial-injustice.rationale: He approved the 1924 law extending U.S. citizenship to Indigenous people born in the country who had been excluded from citizenship, with rights to tribal property preserved.

country-wealth-only-from-land.rationale: In his Massachusetts speeches he treated industrial enterprise, labor, and productive investment as sources of wealth.

courts-bound-by-majority.rationale: Said free government must not degenerate into the unrestrained authority of a mere majority, and that the Declaration's rights cannot be destroyed by any majority.

decide-locally.rationale: The Third Annual Message defended local self-government and called on Congress to guard against intrusion into responsibilities belonging to states and their subdivisions.

democracy-best.rationale: In The Price of Freedom he argued that the people’s errors in government were less dangerous than the errors of autocrats.

direct-votes.rationale: His inaugural address identified legislative representation through Congress as an essential part of republican government. His Boy Scout address described public authority as delegated by the people.

duties-before-rights.rationale: Said any attempt to maintain rights without observing duties is a contradiction of terms and that the duty of obedience needs more emphasis.

dynastic-succession.rationale: Contrasted a system of divine right of rulers by inheritance, where he said there is no real freedom, with self-government. (Moved from monarchy-legitimate, 2026-11-11, when that statement became about ceremonial heads of state.)

elective-rulers.rationale: Said the people have the right to choose their own rulers and that no one has any right to rule over another.

end-foreign-alliances.rationale: Said policy avoids permanent political alliances that sacrifice independence, while having no alliance to end.

entrenched-bill-of-rights.rationale: Held that the Constitution's guaranties can be changed only by amendment with the consent of the States, and praised them as protection of liberty.

equal-moral-worth.rationale: Said the rights of colored citizens are as sacred as any other's, and that the standard applied to inhabitants is manhood, not place of birth.

equal-outcomes.rationale: Said government cannot guarantee a successful life or relieve people of the results of their own folly, and that rewards of industry belong to those who earn them.

expand-fossil-fuels.rationale: He supported keeping federal authority to lease Osage oil lands for extraction at the Secretary of the Interior’s discretion, with attention to supply and market conditions.

farm-price-support.rationale: He returned the McNary–Haugen bill without approval in 1927, rejecting federal intervention to stabilize farm prices through removal of surpluses, and vetoed a revised bill in 1928.

foreign-policy-non-interference.rationale: He sent Marines into Nicaragua’s civil war and dispatched a mediator who negotiated a settlement providing for a U.S.-supervised election.

free-trade.rationale: He used presidential tariff authority to raise duties on lower-priced sewed straw hats to shield domestic manufacturers from lower-cost foreign suppliers.

freedom-is-self-government-of-desire.rationale: In The Price of Freedom he described freedom as requiring self-control and the discipline of self-government, and rejected the idea that freedom consists in doing whatever one wants.

gradual-change.rationale: In the Third Annual Message he favored continuity and gradual improvements, warning that ill-considered government action could impede durable progress.

industrial-civilization-disaster.rationale: He credited industrial production and rising productivity with sustained increases in real wages and a wider distribution of wealth.

labour-priority-over-capital.rationale: In his Massachusetts speeches he treated lawful returns to capital and gains for workers as mutually dependent, with government responsible for justice to both.

legalize-drugs.rationale: He reported federal enforcement of restrictions on intoxicating liquor and narcotics in his First Annual Message.

markets-allocate-better.rationale: Said the government should avoid artificial price support and let economic laws operate; held that business profit is the only basis for wages and employment.

material-conditions-drive-history.rationale: Argued that governments do not make ideals but ideals make governments, and that the Declaration grew from religious teaching.

military-force-beyond-defence.rationale: He deployed Marines in Nicaragua to protect Americans and their property during a civil war abroad.

money-backed-by-precious-metals.rationale: He took the gold-standard side in a public debate during the 1896 free-silver campaign, as he recalled in his autobiography.

more-religion-public.rationale: In his address on church and state he called for greater reliance on religious conviction in public life. He treated religious communities as a source of civic and moral education.

nation-first.rationale: In his First Annual Message he made protection of American interests and freedom of judgment the governing principles of foreign policy, with international cooperation undertaken on those terms.

natural-rulers.rationale: Held that if no one is born into a superior station there is no ruling class and authority must rest on the people.

night-watchman-state.rationale: He signed legislation regulating radio broadcasting and accepted a federal role in flood relief and reconstruction.

no-central-bank.rationale: He signed the McFadden Act, which made the charters of the Federal Reserve Banks permanent.

no-duty-to-obey.rationale: Taught that obedience to law is the first duty of a citizen and that more emphasis must be placed on it, starting in the home and school.

office-by-exam.rationale: In his Second Annual Message he praised competitive civil-service selection and urged extending the classified system to postmasters and several other federal offices.

open-borders.rationale: He approved permanent immigration quotas and categorical exclusions in the Immigration Act of 1924.

pay-off-national-debt.rationale: In his Third Annual Message he urged retiring the principal of the war debt as early as possible, pointing to earlier federal debts that had been paid off. He reiterated the aim of clearing the debt in his Fifth Annual Message.

pool-sovereignty.rationale: Said the country could not barter away its independence or sovereignty even while joining the World Court.

preserve-national-culture.rationale: In his First Annual Message he insisted that American institutions depended on retaining a distinct national civic tradition and wanted immigration limited to the capacity to integrate new arrivals.

profit-exploitation.rationale: Said employment and wages depend on someone making a profit, which is the sound basis of distribution; denying profit denies the reward of thrift.

promote-democracy-abroad.rationale: He dispatched Henry Stimson to mediate the Nicaraguan civil war and provided U.S. personnel to supervise the competitive election agreed upon at the settlement.

property-fundamental.rationale: Said the Constitution guarantees the right to hold property, great and small, and that the people's title to it is absolute; but put rights of persons first.

property-serves-common-good.rationale: Said owners of property are charged with a service and that these duties carry divine sanction, though he also called property title absolute.

public-ownership.rationale: Opposed government ownership of coal mines, urged sale of the government merchant fleet to private owners and of Muscle Shoals, and said public ownership cannot distribute wealth.

race-based-immigration-restrictions.rationale: He approved the 1924 immigration law, which barred aliens ineligible for citizenship when naturalization eligibility was defined on racial grounds.

racial-pride.rationale: Wished false and ignorant prejudice to be replaced with a 'true and enlightened pride of race'.

reduce-immigration.rationale: He approved the 1924 law imposing strict national-origin quotas and excluding immigrants who were racially ineligible for naturalization.

regulate-corporations.rationale: In the Fourth Annual Message he called for reducing federal bureaus that regulate business and for restricting federal intervention to abuses that required it.

revolution-legitimate.rationale: At the Declaration anniversary he endorsed American independence as a legitimate popular assertion of the right to choose one’s rulers.

separated-powers.rationale: Credited the three independent branches with checks on each other as the guarantees of liberty.

small-step-social-reform.rationale: In his Third Annual Message he advocated moderation and improving established policies through changes in detail.

state-harmful.rationale: Described government as the people's agent whose proper role is limited, yet defended it as the means of liberty and order.

state-supports-good-ways-of-life.rationale: He asked federal officials to develop a national policy expanding outdoor recreation because he considered it a way to build physical health and moral character.

tariffs-protect-industry.rationale: He used the flexible tariff authority to raise the duty on lower-priced imported sewed straw hats from 60 to 88 percent to offset the domestic producers’ higher costs.

tax-inheritance.rationale: The tax legislation he championed and signed reduced federal inheritance taxes.

tax-the-wealthy.rationale: He championed and signed income-tax reductions that sharply lowered surtaxes on large incomes while retaining progressive rates.

taxation-theft.rationale: Called taxes not needed for public necessity 'a species of legalized larceny' but accepted that tax ministering to public necessity is constitutional, so he did not treat taxation itself as theft.

unions-good.rationale: He secured Massachusetts laws protecting trade unions and signed the Railway Labor Act, which protected railroad workers’ ability to organize. In the Boston police strike he mobilized the State Guard and refused to support reinstatement of striking officers.

unlimited-reelection.rationale: Favored the long-established custom against a third presidential term, and held that one man can hardly serve the country well beyond eight years.

wages-fall-to-bare-minimum.rationale: His Sixth Annual Message rejected the idea that the wage fund is fixed and argued that growth in production can increase real wages, citing increases across U.S. industries.

wealth-concentration-endangers-liberty.rationale: Asked whether any prosperity or commercial instrument can be too great, and argued wealth is the product of industry; condemned only wealth assembled for unlawful purposes.

women-suffrage.rationale: As a Massachusetts legislator he supported a resolution for woman suffrage and identified it as part of his legislative record.

notes: This pass searched the annual messages, Massachusetts addresses, autobiography, presidential speeches, and published records for economic policy, labor, government, foreign affairs, civil liberties, culture, social policy, conservation, technology, and political methods. The record distinguishes Coolidge’s protection of private-sector collective bargaining from his intervention in the Boston police strike. The 1924 Immigration Act used national-origin quotas and excluded immigrants deemed racially ineligible for naturalization.

booksNotUsed.reason: Both addresses chiefly recount and commemorate Washington’s leadership. The Declaration anniversary address states Coolidge’s own position on the legitimacy of independence more directly.

The Mount Rushmore address commemorates four presidents and the national founding. Its historical treatment of westward expansion does not settle a position on removing Indigenous people from their lands.
